short_description: Prevents the container from running with full host-level access instead of a sandboxed container
cis_remediation_notes: Add policies to each namespace in the cluster which has user workloads to restrict the admission of privileged containers as they have access to all Linux Kernel capabilities and devices. A container running with full privileges can do almost everything that the host can do.

short_description: Prevents the container from seeing and potentially interacting with every process on the host machine
cis_remediation_notes:
Configure the Admission Controller to restrict the admission of hostPID containers .A container running in the host's PID namespace can inspect processes running outside the container  which can be used to
escalate privileges of the container.

short_description: Prevents the container from sharing the host's network namespace directly
cis_remediation_notes: Add policies to each namespace in the cluster which has user workloads to restrict the admission of hostNetwork containers as a container running in the host's network namespace could access the local loopback device and access network traffic to and from other pods.

short_description: Ensures the container process runs as a non-root user instead of root inside the container
cis_remediation_notes:
Create a policy for each namespace in the cluster that ensures  
MustRunAsNonRoot with the range of UIDs not including 0, is set. Containers which run as the root user, have a escalated likelihood of
container breakout.

short_description: Prevents a process from gaining more privileges than its parent process had
cis_remediation_notes:
Add policies to each namespace in the cluster to restrict the
admission of containers with securityContext: allowPrivilegeEscalation: true such container may have processes that can gain more privileges than their parent.

short_description: Ensures CPU/memory limits are set so one container cannot starve resources from others on the node
cis_remediation_notes: Limiting the scope of user permissions can reduce the impact of mistakes or malicious activities.

short_description: Grants only the specific API actions needed instead of unrestricted access to all actions
cis_remediation_notes:
The principle of least privilege recommends that users are provided only the access
required for their role and nothing more. The use of wildcard rights grants is likely to
provide excessive rights to the Kubernetes API.

short_description: Grants access only to the specific resource types needed instead of every resource type in the cluster
cis_remediation_notes:
The principle of least privilege recommends that users are provided only the access
required for their role and nothing more. The use of wildcard rights grants is likely to
provide excessive rights to the Kubernetes API.

short_description: Limits what can be done with Secrets specifically -- broad access to secrets is a common path to credential theft
cis_remediation_notes:
Inappropriate access to secrets stored within the Kubernetes cluster can allow for an
attacker to gain additional access to the cluster or external resources with secret credentials.hence, restrict access to secret objects in the cluster by removing get, list, and watch permissions.

short_description: Binds the role to one specific service account instead of every authenticated user/service in the cluster
cis_remediation_notes: When a pod is created, if a service account is not specify, it is automatically assigned the default service account in the same namespace. Make  own service account and let the API server manage its security tokens.

short_description: Binds to a narrowly scoped custom role instead of Kubernetes' built-in all-powerful cluster-admin role
cis_remediation_notes: Cluster-admin provide wide-ranging privileges like  allow super-user access to perform any action on any resource,which should only be applied where absolutely necessary.

short_description: Ensures both ingress AND egress rules are actually enforced -- an egress rule with no matching policyType silently does nothing
cis_remediation_notes: If the CNI plugin in use does not support network policies, consideration should be given to making use of a different plugin, or finding an alternate mechanism for restricting traffic in the Kubernetes cluster.

short_description: Restricts which pods can send traffic in instead of allowing traffic from any source
cis_remediation_notes:
Network segmentation is important to ensure that containers can communicate only with those they are supposed
to as running different applications on the same Kubernetes cluster creates a risk of one compromised application attacking a neighbor.

short_description: Restricts which destinations the pod can send traffic to instead of allowing traffic to anywhere
cis_remediation_notes:
When a network policy is introduced to a given namespace, all traffic not allowed by the policy is denied. However, if there are no network policies in a namespace all traffic will be allowed into and out of the pods in that
namespace.

short_description: Scopes the policy to the specific workload it's meant to protect instead of applying broadly to all pods in the namespace
cis_remediation_notes:
Network Policies are namespace scoped. When a network policy is introduced to a
given namespace, all traffic not allowed by the policy is denied. However, if there are no
network policies in a namespace all traffic will be allowed into and out of the pods in that
namespace.
